Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday that he feared his US counterpart Donald Trump "will continue" lifitng sanctions on Russia. Zelensky's relationship with Trump deteriorated after the Washington eased sanctions on Moscow as part of a diesel-supply deal, despite Russia increasing strikes on Ukraine.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Saturday that he feared the United States would lift more sanctions on Russia and that President Donald Trump's action only "rewards" Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.
Trump heightened a battle with Zelensky on Friday when he signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions targeting Russia's energy revenues.
The decision came despite Russia increasing strikes on Ukraine in the fifth year of its war, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
Trump had already announced that he had agreed to a deal with Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions, and Zelensky said he feared more concessions.
"Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelensky told reporters.
He said he still "personally" hoped that Trump will do "everything in his power" to make Putin end the war but added: "You cannot achieve this by limiting Ukraine's responses to Russia for killing our people. And certainly not by lifting sanctions."
Ukraine said at least two people were killed in Russian air strikes on Saturday.
$80 billion in funding for Ukraine
Earlier on Friday, Zelensky urged EU leaders to keep financing Kyiv's fight with nearly $80 billion more next year, as he insisted he was standing up for his country amid the fresh row with US Trump.
Trump branded Kyiv's actions a "disgrace" and said it was easier to deal with Putin than Zelensky, after the Ukrainian leader ordered his forces to resume strikes on Russian refineries.

"I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively," Zelensky told journalists after talks with EU leaders in Brussels.
Asked if he was being made a scapegoat for Trump's domestic woes ahead of the US midterms, Zelensky just smiled.
"This is my answer," he said, after an extended pregnant pause.
The latest breakdown between Trump and Zelensky has fuelled fear that the US leader is siding with Moscow.
Those concerns have been heightened by disruptions to a critical US-provided satellite system that has hampered Ukraine's ability to counter Russia's intense bombardments.
Ukraine uses the Starshield system from Elon Musk's SpaceX for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones. It also uses SpaceX's parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, but not for offensive operations.
Tech billionaire Musk – though a virulent Zelensky critic – said his company was not behind the disruption and a US official denied any intervention by Trump.

"Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes," Zelensky said.
In his speech to EU leaders, Zelensky said that he believed that most Americans supported Ukraine's fight against Moscow's invasion.
"At the end of the day, the American people will have their say," he said.
70 billion-euro question
While he grapples with Trump, European leaders put on a show of unity with Zelensky.
"This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions," European Council chief Antonio Costa said.
"Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure."
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that "the situation in Ukraine is currently truly dire, with numerous Russian attacks and a tense relationship between Ukraine and the US."
"It is crucial that we, as Europe, demonstrate our unconditional support for them today – and explore what additional steps we can take," he said.

But the EU leaders will need to find more than just words to keep Ukraine going.
Zelensky asked the bloc to provide more Patriot missiles to shoot down Russian missiles and come up with an extra €70 billion ($79 billion) in support next year to help Kyiv keep fighting.
"This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back."
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen confirmed that the figure of €70 billion "has to be covered" and urged partner countries to "step in" and help. Leaders told her commission to come up with a proposal for the financing.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Kyiv's backers will analyse the demand, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the EU will discuss it before the end of the year.
Macron also said Europe was "working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed."
Frozen assets
The EU is currently paying out instalments of a €90 billion loan for Kyiv that was set to help cover funding to the end of 2027.
But the Ukrainian authorities have warned they will still face a major budget black hole as Russian strikes have battered the country's economy.
The talks on new funding have reignited calls for the European Union to tap around 200 billion euros in frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.
"The frozen assets are there. That's what should be used for supporting Ukraine," said Latvian premier Andris Kulbergs.
But there seems little momentum on that front as Belgium, where most of the funds are held, remains opposed.

high_priority_articles.title: Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas? - Al Jazeera
high_priority_articles.summary: Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas?  Al JazeeraU.S. President wants 60 days to analyse impact of Russia sanctions law, says Marco Rubio  The Hindu‘India diversified imports, but hard to pivot in one day’: Marco Rubio explains why US waived some Russia energy tariffs  Hindustan TimesPause on Trump’s punitive tariffs gives India relief, but trade uncertainty persists  Telegraph IndiaChristmas cheer, but caution remains:...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order waiving newly-passed Russia sanctions, claiming the move is in the US’s “national interest”.
Earlier this month, Trump also announced a deal to bring stocks of Russian diesel into global markets, in a bid to drive down energy prices that have spiked during the US-Israel war on Iran. The US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027.
Trump’s embrace of Russian energy has angered Ukraine, European partners and many US officials, who say the move rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war against its neighbour.
Ukraine’s President Volodmyr Zelenskyy slammed Trump’s diesel deal as “a gift” to Russia’s President Vladimir Putin that will help fund his war effort.
While European countries have also criticised Trump’s embrace of Russian energy, the US president has accused them of “hypocrisy”, as figures show that European Union countries continue to import Russian gas.
Here’s what we know:
Which sanctions has Trump waived?
In his executive order on Friday, Trump called off numerous planned Russia-related sanctions days before they were due to take effect, including duties on Russian goods and penalties for buying the country’s oil and gas.
The now-blocked measures were part of legislation passed in Congress with bipartisan support last month, named after the late US Senator Lindsay Graham, an outspoken critic of Russia.
They would have included up to 100 percent tariffs on all goods brought into the US from the five top importers of Russian crude oil or gas, including China and India. They could also have imposed equal penalties on countries deemed to have knowingly bought oil or gas from Russia 30 days after the law’s implementation, or to be among the top five countries helping Moscow circumvent sanctions on sales of its oil.
The waiver will hold until the Trump administration believes “further action is appropriate”, according to the executive order.
US Congressman Don Beyer, a Democrat from Virginia, said the sanctions waiver amounts to a “surrender to Putin” that “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent”.
Who will benefit from this?
Vasily Astrov, an economist at the Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Russian government will likely be the greatest beneficiary because the easing of sanctions means Russian oil will not have to be further discounted.
He estimated that about 60 cents of every extra dollar in the price of a barrel of Russian oil would “end up in state coffers”.
Russian official Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy for Putin, hailed the US decision to waive the sanctions as “an important and truly historic moment”.
Other beneficiaries include major importers of Russian oil and gas, such as China and India, who are now less exposed to the risk of secondary US penalties.
While Trump hopes the measures will also help bring down oil prices for US consumers before November mid-term elections, experts say that is less certain.
Addressing the US’s recent diesel deal with Russia, EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis said it is unlikely to have a significant impact on global prices.
According to Trump, that deal would bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel into US and global markets “immediately”, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November, and 1 million tonnes afterwards.
“If we look at the volumes, they are not of any macroeconomic significance, and frankly, there are strong doubts whether Russia is even able to supply those volumes, and according also to US quality standards, those are big question marks,” Dombrovskis told the AFP news agency.
Which countries still buy oil from Russia?
China and India are the largest buyers of Russian crude oil, purchasing 6 billion euros ($6.74bn) and 3.6 billion euros ($4.04bn) worth respectively in September, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a nonprofit think tank.
Hungary and Slovakia, the landlocked EU members that have exemptions to the bloc’s ban on Russian crude, also remain big customers, buying a combined 290 million euros ($326m) worth of the commodity in September, said CREA. Turkiye imported 172 million euros ($193m) worth of Russian crude oil the same month, the think tank added.
Since the end of 2022, the largest importers of Russian oil products, which include diesel, have been Turkiye, China, Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Singapore.
Saudi Arabia imported the most Russian oil products in September at 534 million euros ($600m), followed by Turkiye with 321 million euros ($361m), China with 304 million euros ($342m) and India with 161 million euros ($181m).
Is Europe buying increasing amounts of gas from Russia?
“The European Council regrets the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel,” European leaders said in a joint statement adopted following a two-day European Council meeting in Brussels this week.
But despite its own near-blanket ban on Russian oil, the EU has continued to import large quantities of Russian gas, though it plans to phase out those imports next year.
Urgewald, a Germany-based group that researches coal companies, reported this week that more than 12 million tonnes of Russian Arctic LNG was transported into EU ports from January to September this year, a 9.5 percent jump from the same period last year.
In September, EU countries imported 817 million euros ($918m) of pipeline gas, and 615 million euros ($691m) of liquefied natural gas (LNG), according to CREA.
EU members France and the Netherlands were the largest LNG importers, bringing in 446 million euros ($501m) and 116 million euros ($130m) respectively, according to the think tank. France’s LNG imports represented a 103 percent increase from the previous month, it added.
France’s President Emmanuel Macron has been among the most outspoken about Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, saying on Friday that it “sends a negative message” and would have no impact on global prices.
Hungary imported the most Russian pipeline gas of any EU member by far during the month, with 414 million euros ($465m) worth. Slovakia and Bulgaria brought in 161 million euros ($181m) and 132 million euros ($148m), respectively, according to CREA data.

high_priority_articles.summary: UK, France, and Germany Gear Up for Ukraine Deployment With Major Military Drills in Poland  UNITED24 Media'Mystery drones over UK' and 'Troops heading to Poland for war games'  BBCHundreds of British troops to rehearse Ukraine mission  The TimesBritish troops to take part in major Ukraine-facing wargame next month  The IndependentNATO troops to train in Poland for potential peacekeeping duties in Ukraine  TVP World
high_priority_articles.full_text:
At least 1,500 troops from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Poland are expected to participate in military exercises in Poland in November, rehearsing the deployment of a multinational force to Ukraine following a potential ceasefire with Russia.
According to The Times on October 17, the exercises will focus on preparing European forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine as part of security arrangements intended to deter renewed Russian aggression.
The drills will test the movement of military personnel, coordination between national armed forces, and the delivery of essential supplies, including fuel and food. These logistical preparations are considered necessary for any future deployment of European troops to Ukrainian territory.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed that thousands of military personnel would take part in the exercises next month. Streeting said the training would help participating countries prepare to support Ukraine’s military training requirements and post-war reconstruction.
The planned exercises form part of the Coalition of the Willing initiative, which brings together countries working on potential security guarantees for Ukraine following a cessation of hostilities.
According to The Times, the training will bring multinational units together to practice operating alongside one another, with particular attention to the practical requirements of moving and sustaining troops across borders.
The coalition’s plans have developed through a series of discussions between Ukraine and its European partners over the possible deployment of an international security contingent.
In January 2026, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, and France signed a declaration of intent concerning the potential deployment of multinational forces following a peace agreement. The proposed mission would support Ukraine’s defense capabilities, military training, and long-term security.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Money moved fast this week. Traders watched two inflation reports land back to back, and Polymarket news today shows just how shaky their confidence got. One prediction market swung from calm to chaos and back again in 48 hours. The crypto market felt it too, with prices sliding as the odds flipped. Here’s exactly what happened, what the numbers say, and what the Federal Reserve might do next.
Key Takeaways
This week’s Polymarket news today centers on one simple fact: inflation refuses to cool down. The Kobeissi Letter reported that US CPI inflation climbed to 3.7%, nearly double the Fed’s 2% target. US PPI inflation jumped even higher, to 6.3%, over three times that target. Core PPI, which strips out food and energy, reached 5.0%, two and a half times the Fed’s goal.
September marked the 67th straight month that CPI inflation stayed above the Fed’s 2% target. The US dollar has lost nearly a quarter of its value over the past five years, per the same report. Numbers like these don’t just move bond yields. They move Polymarket odds too, and this one reacted within hours of each release.
The ripple reached crypto as well. CoinGecko data shows the global crypto market cap sitting at $2.83 trillion today, down 0.8% over the last 24 hours.
Source: Coingecko Data
Daily trading volume stands at $75.87 billion, while Bitcoin dominance holds at 57.7% and Ethereum dominance sits at 10.4%. Prices surged before the data, shook once the numbers hit, and are cooling off again now.
That’s the real story behind Polymarket news today: a single market called “Fed Decision in October” that moved harder than anyone expected.
Source: Official Site
| Timing | No Change Odds | 25 bps Hike Odds | 
|---|---|---|
| Before CPI & PPI (pre-Oct 15) | 80-81% | 19-20% | 
| Between CPI & PPI (Oct 15-16) | 52-72% | 28-48% | 
| After Both Reports (post-Oct 16) | 87% | 14% | 
Before the data dropped, bettors felt comfortable. No change looked like the safe bet at 80-81%. Once CPI landed, then PPI followed a day later, confidence cracked. Hike odds nearly tripled at one point, hitting 48%.
But once both reports were fully priced in, the odds snapped back toward 87% for no change and just 14% for a hike. The market shook, then steadied.
Not everyone panicked. On Polymarket’s separate “How many rate cuts in 2026” question, the odds barely moved before, during, or after the inflation reports. No rate cut held at 96.9% (roughly 97%) the entire time. A single 25 bps cut sat at just 0.8%.
Source: Official Website
Hot CPI and PPI prints shook the October decision odds, but this longer-term market shrugged them off completely.
Context matters here. The Federal Reserve hadn’t raised rates since July 2023. That changed on September 16, 2026, when the FOMC voted 12-0 to hike rates by 25 basis points, pushing the range to 3.75%-4.00%. Rates were cut back in December 2025, so September’s move was the first change in either direction since then.
That single vote is the backdrop every Polymarket bettor is now pricing against.
So where does this leave things? Polymarket’s current data points to no change at the next two meetings:
That’s the prediction today, not a guarantee. Betting markets can flip fast, as this very week proved. One more hot inflation print could reopen the hike debate before either date arrives.
Expert Opinion: Market analysts note that prediction markets like Polymarket tend to overreact to single data points before drifting back toward their baseline, a pattern visible in this week’s swing from 81% to 52% and back to 87%. The gap between hot inflation data and steady long-term rate-cut prediction suggests bettors still trust the Fed’s September hike to do its job, at least for now. Analysts add that one more hot CPI or PPI print could easily reopen the hike debate before October 28.
Polymarket news today paints a clear picture: traders expect the Fed to hold steady at its October 28 and December 9 meetings, even with inflation running hot. Prediction markets move fast, though, and nothing is locked in until they actually votes. Watch the data, not the headlines.

high_priority_articles.title: UK inflation can seal the deal on BOE’s November rate hike - The Edge Malaysia
high_priority_articles.summary: UK inflation can seal the deal on BOE’s November rate hike  The Edge Malaysia
high_priority_articles.full_text:
(Oct 18): A pickup in UK inflation to a nine-month high in data this week is likely to set the stage for key decisions from the upcoming budget to a likely interest-rate increase.
The report on Wednesday is anticipated by economists to show annual price growth in September at 3.4%. The result will amount to a reality check for British policymakers returning to London after warm words and an upgraded growth forecast from the International Monetary Fund.
The inflation data are likely to help seal the deal on the first rate hike from the Bank of England in over three years in November, while also feeding into the thinking of Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey, who has vowed to give businesses and households some “breathing space” at next week’s budget.
His fiscal plans are being hemmed in by the global bond rout after the resurgence in energy prices prompted traders to bet on a series of BOE rate increases to contain inflationary pressures.
Gilt yields have risen to around their highest levels in decades, eroding Healey’s already-thin fiscal wiggle room. Tax hikes are likely to be needed to fund any cost-of-living measures, with banks set to be targeted.
While the BOE has held off on raising borrowing costs so far, investors are betting on it joining the Federal Reserve and European Central Bank in tightening policy at its upcoming meeting on Nov 5.
“The combination of soaring inflation, resilient demand and a stabilising labour market will make it hard for the BOE to remain on hold. We expect a 25-basis-point hike at the central bank’s next meeting in November. We also see another move in February,” said Bloomberg Economics.
Governor Andrew Bailey said in Bangkok last week that there is little evidence the energy shock is spreading widely across the economy yet, and figures on Tuesday will also likely suggest that price pressures from the labor market remain muted.
But the inflation situation is predicted to get worse. Bailey warned that the longer the Middle East conflict drags on, the more difficult it’s becoming to avoid a hike. The UK central bank is already forecasting that inflation will top 4% in early 2027, double its 2% target.
Elsewhere, Chinese growth data, Japanese inflation, global purchasing manager indexes and a rate decision from the embattled Indonesian central bank may be among the highlights.
Below is our wrap of what is coming up in the global economy.
In the wake of fresh inflation figures that showed price pressures are accelerating, the US economic data calendar lightens up. On Tuesday, separate reports on new residential construction and pending sales of previously owned homes are projected to illustrate the housing market was still struggling for traction in September.
Affordability constraints continue to weigh on demand, with 30-year mortgage rates recently hitting an almost three-year high of 7.5%.
On Friday, S&P Global will release its preliminary October manufacturing and services indexes. Economists see both measures pointing to solid growth, yet at a slightly slower pace. The same day, the University of Michigan releases its final October consumer sentiment reading.
Federal Reserve policymakers are in a media blackout period ahead of the Oct 27-28 policy meeting.
In Canada, Monday’s inflation update and business outlook will provide the final major clues to how the economy is weathering oil-driven inflation risks and the fallout from escalating trade tensions before policymakers make their next rate decision on Oct 28.
Headline yearly change in the consumer price index has held near 3% for months, which Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem has called “too high.” Economists expect it accelerated in September to 3.2%, though core measures likely held steady.
Meanwhile, retail sales likely rebounded in August after a temporary slump in July, though the resurgence may be short lived.
Albertans will vote Monday in a referendum that asks whether they’d like to begin a process to separate from Canada. The “remain” side holds a comfortable lead, but federalists fear high turnout for separation will introduce political and economics risks.
Later in the week, Prime Minister Mark Carney will travel to Türkiye to advance talks for a comprehensive trade agreement.
China releasing key economic data and several central banks lining up monetary policy decisions take the spotlight in Asia-Pacific this week.
China releases its third-quarter gross domestic product alongside September retail sales, industrial production, fixed-asset investment and property data on Monday. The figures will show the economic momentum in the world’s second-largest economy amid a prolonged property downturn that continues to weigh on investment.
China’s one-year and five-year loan prime rates on Tuesday are expected to stay unchanged at 3% and 3.5%, respectively. Industrial production data due Monday will also help gauge manufacturing activity in the country.
Indonesia is expected to keep its policy rate unchanged at 5.75% on Wednesday, while the Philippines is seen raising 25 basis points on Thursday. Rate-hike pressures prevail in South Korea too. The decisions will be closely watched as officials across the region balance inflation and currency pressures against risks to growth.
Inflation and business activity put Japan in focus on Friday. National CPI will offer another indication of whether price pressures remain strong enough to support the Bank of Japan’s historic policy-normalisation path.
Japan’s flash PMIs the same day will show whether growth remains broad-based across manufacturing and services. Trade data on Wednesday will provide another gauge of external demand.
Flash PMIs are also due in India that day. They will be closely watched for signs of how the economy is coping with a difficult external environment as inflation firms and oil prices remain above US$100 (RM408) a barrel. Core industries output, due Wednesday, will provide an earlier read on industrial momentum.
Elsewhere, South Korea’s early trade data and Taiwan’s export orders will help investors assess the strength of the regional trade and technology cycle.
Reserve Bank of Australia assistant governor Christopher Kent is due for an interview on News24 on Sunday and a fireside chat on Monday. RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser is due to make an appearance on Wednesday.
Germany’s ZEW investor confidence survey is due on Tuesday. The euro region’s first PMIs from the final quarter of the year will be a highlight, with those numbers on Friday seen likely to show resilient expansion. The European Central Bank’s survey of consumer expectations comes out the same day.
Few policymakers are on the calendar after last week’s IMF meetings, and a blackout period in advance of the Oct 29 rate decision will kick in on Wednesday.
France will continue to draw attention for its extended budget troubles. The country has been on negative outlook at Moody’s Ratings for a year, raising the prospect that a review result scheduled for Friday will lead to a downgrade.
Away from the eurozone, Hungary is due to unveil its 2027 budget at the start of the week, giving first concrete indications of how it plans to more than halve its deficit to the 3% required to join by the euro.
Meanwhile on Thursday, the Swiss National Bank will publish a summary of its September decision, when officials kept borrowing costs unchanged while dialling down their threat of franc intervention.
In South Africa, data on Wednesday will likely show inflation accelerated in September as fuel prices continue to climb.
Later in the day, Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana will present his medium-term budget in Cape Town, with investors looking for signs of commitment to repairing the public finances through a fiscal anchor. They also expect progress on consolidation, helped by mining-tax revenue and a narrower-than-expected deficit.
A number of monetary decisions are scheduled:
The August GDP-proxy report from Argentina will likely add fresh evidence that the economy is on track to enter a technical recession, which would be the second under President Javier Milei.
Local economists now forecast third-quarter output at -1% — down from a forecast of 1.1% growth just a month ago — in the wake of July’s GDP-proxy report that showed the economy taking its steepest tumble since April 2020.
In Colombia, August’s 7.4-magnitude quake that struck the western part of the country will weigh heavily on the month’s economic activity data. Extensive damage from the temblor is expected to damp growth into 2027 before rebuilding gives the economy a boost.
Mexico offers up myriad growth indicators in the coming week, with GDP-proxy figures, joblessness and retail sales, which are likely to underscore the economy’s resilience.
Early October consumer prices data — the last inflation figures policymakers will get before their Nov 5 rate decision — aren’t likely to alarm or assure Banxico’s board.
Paraguay’s central bank has been on hold since a quarter-point cut in February put the key rate at 5.5%. Annual inflation ticked up to 1.7% in September though policymakers project it ending the year near the 3.5% center of their target range.
Rounding out the week in economic reports, Brazil on Friday publishes its mid-October consumer prices report ahead of Sunday’s presidential run-off election. Polling shows that the race has tightened up, but Senator Flávio Bolsonaro still appears poised to deny President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva his bid for a fourth term.
On the inflation front, the early consensus sees the annual print rising beyond the 4.5% ceiling of the central bank’s target range, perhaps nearing 4.8.
Economists in the central bank’s Oct 9 survey raised their 2026 inflation estimate for Latin America’s biggest economy to 5.22%, a 21 basis-point rise over the previous survey.

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said the central bank will not tolerate underlying inflation running above its 2% target and will press ahead with interest rate increases.
Ueda made the remarks at a news conference on the 16th in Bangkok, where finance ministers and central bank governors of the Group of 20 were meeting, according to the Nihon Keizai Shimbun, Reuters and other foreign media on the 17th.
"Underlying inflation is broadly close to our 2% target, so we cannot tolerate it rising further," Ueda said. "Our policy stance has recently shifted into a phase in which anchoring inflation near the 2% target becomes an important policy goal." On financial conditions, Ueda said the environment has remained accommodative even after last month's rate increase, adding that the central bank "will continue to adjust the degree of easing by raising the policy rate." He said the BOJ would review the issue at its next monetary policy meeting.
The comments came ahead of a key BOJ monetary policy meeting later this month. Board members will present new quarterly projections for growth and prices at the gathering, which markets are expected to scrutinize for clues on the pace and timing of further rate increases. At last month's meeting, the BOJ raised its short-term policy rate, the benchmark, by 0.25 percentage points to about 1.25% from about 1.0%.
Financial markets largely expect the BOJ to hold rates steady at this month's meeting, with attention turning to whether it will deliver another increase at its December gathering, the Nikkei reported. Reuters, citing sources, said many within the central bank favor keeping rates unchanged at the meeting later this month and waiting for more data showing how the increases so far have affected the economy and financial conditions, while adding that the BOJ is expected to send hawkish signals leaving the door open to a December hike.

high_priority_articles.title: Trump again pushes Saudi Arabia to Accept Israel’s Help against Houthis - Daily Pakistan
high_priority_articles.summary: Trump again pushes Saudi Arabia to Accept Israel’s Help against Houthis  Daily Pakistan
high_priority_articles.full_text:
ISLAMABAD – US President Donald Trump made a striking pitch to Saudi Arabia to accept Israel’s help against Yemen’s Houthi rebels.
Calling Israeli support very helpful, Trump hinted that a Saudi-Israeli normalization deal could be closer than ever, even as Riyadh maintains that Palestinian statehood remains key and Iran offers to help end the conflict.
US President Donald Trump urged Saudi Arabia to accept Israel’s assistance against Yemen’s Houthi rebels, adding a new dimension to regional tensions as speculation grows over a possible normalization agreement between Riyadh and Tel Aviv.
Trump was asked whether Saudi Arabia should accept Israeli support in operations against the Houthis. “Yes, absolutely. Israel has been very helpful to Saudi Arabia,” he replied, hinting at cooperation between two countries amid continuing regional security concerns.
Trump’s remarks also revived questions about whether Saudi Arabia could move closer to formally normalizing relations with Israel, a diplomatic breakthrough that has remained elusive despite previous efforts backed by Washington.
Asked whether Saudi Arabia’s potential entry into the Abraham Accords was being reconsidered, Trump expressed optimism, saying, “Yes, I think it could happen. Perhaps it is even more likely than before.” He called Abraham Accords “one of our great achievements,” referring to the agreements brokered through US efforts in 2020 that established or normalized relations between Israel and several Arab countries.
Trump further claimed that Saudi Arabia was pleased with the support of both Israel and the United States.
Before Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, Saudi Arabia and Israel had been widely viewed as moving closer to a possible normalization agreement. However, the diplomatic landscape has since been complicated by the Gaza war and the wider regional conflict.
Riyadh has consistently maintained that clear progress toward the establishment of a Palestinian state is necessary for normalizing relations with Israel, making the future of any agreement dependent on broader political and security considerations.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also made comments that have drawn attention to the possibility of regional cooperation. Asked in an interview with Israeli media on Tuesday whether Saudi Arabia had requested assistance from Israel, Netanyahu responded, according to The Times of Israel, “There is hardly a state in the Middle East that is not asking us for help.”
His remarks came amid heightened attention to the security implications of Houthi activities and the potential role of Israel in addressing threats facing countries across the region.
However, Netanyahu’s statement, as reported, did not explicitly confirm that Saudi Arabia had formally requested Israeli assistance.

high_priority_articles.title: Did Trump Lift Russia Sanctions? What the October 16 Waiver Changes - Diplomacy and Law
high_priority_articles.summary: Did Trump Lift Russia Sanctions? What the October 16 Waiver Changes  Diplomacy and Law
high_priority_articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump did not lift the broader U.S. sanctions regime against Russia on October 16, 2026. His Russia sanctions waiver suspended major measures under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, including an additional 500% tariff on Russian goods and 100% tariffs on imports from countries meeting specified criteria for Russian energy purchases or sanctions evasion. The executive order waived these additional duties before they took effect, rather than removing tariffs that had already been collected (White House, 2026).
The decision also covered new restrictions concerning Russian financial institutions, investment, energy transactions, and sovereign debt. Not every provision was awaiting implementation: the Graham Act's prohibition on purchases of Russian sovereign debt by U.S. persons had already taken effect when the legislation was enacted on September 18. Earlier executive-order sanctions, including applicable asset freezes and financial prohibitions administered by the Office of Foreign Assets Control, remain enforceable. The Graham Act itself was neither repealed nor permanently terminated (United States Congress, 2026; White House, 2026).
The waiver came two days before the October 18 deadline for implementing the additional tariffs and contains no fixed expiration date. It remains effective until the President or Secretary of State, following the prescribed consultations, determines that further action is appropriate. For major purchasers of Russian energy, particularly China and India, and other significant importers such as Turkey, the decision suspends prospective American tariff pressure without establishing that any of these countries had been formally identified for the proposed 100% duties. It also limits the additional economic pressure Congress intended to impose on Moscow during Russia's continuing war against Ukraine.
The international legal consequences depend on the distinction between American sanctions, European Union restrictive measures, and sanctions imposed by the United Nations Security Council. EU restrictions operate under an independent legal framework, while binding Security Council measures derive their authority from the UN Charter. The Security Council has not established a comprehensive sanctions regime against Russia in response to its invasion of Ukraine, although individual Russian persons or entities may be subject to other UN sanctions regimes. Washington's October 16 decision cannot terminate European restrictions or alter independently binding Security Council obligations. Its legal effect remains confined to the American measures covered by the waiver.
1. What Did Trump's October 16 Waiver Suspend?
President Donald Trump's executive order of October 16, 2026, waived substantial sanctions and trade restrictions established under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. Enacted on September 18, the legislation introduced additional measures targeting Russian financial institutions, energy transactions, investment, and international trade. Section 115 authorized the President to waive specified obligations after submitting a national-interest certification and explanatory report to Congress (United States Congress, 2026).
Section 4 of the executive order exercises that authority across several provisions of the Act. The decision covers the proposed 500% tariff on Russian goods, additional 100% tariffs affecting qualifying third countries, and restrictions involving Russian financial and commercial activities. Although many measures were scheduled for implementation within 30 days of enactment, others had different commencement rules.
The order suspended the application of specified statutory measures without repealing the legislation. It also retained responsibilities for monitoring Russian energy purchases and sanctions evasion, allowing the administration to reconsider the waivers. The distinction is significant because the October 16 decision changed the immediate enforcement of the Graham Act while preserving the possibility of future action under its provisions (White House, 2026, Sections 3–4).
1.1 The Suspended 500% Tariff on Russian Imports
Section 112 of the Graham Act provided for an additional duty of up to 500% ad valorem on goods imported into the United States from Russia. Its coverage extended to merchandise generally, including energy products, subject to statutory exceptions. Section 2(a) of the October 16 executive order specified the 500% rate, but Section 4(a) simultaneously waived its application (United States Congress, 2026, Section 112; White House, 2026, Sections 2 and 4).
The proposed duty would have operated alongside other applicable customs charges. Its economic significance was the substantial additional cost it could have imposed on Russian merchandise entering the American market. However, the tariff was waived before implementation, and no additional duty was collected under the new measure.
The waiver does not eliminate earlier restrictions affecting Russian imports. Products prohibited under independent sanctions authorities remain subject to those prohibitions, while other applicable customs duties continue to operate. For Russian exporters, the October 16 decision removed a prospective additional trade barrier without restoring access to goods or transactions already restricted under American law.
1.2 The 100% Tariffs on Buyers of Russian Energy
Section 113 established a separate tariff mechanism intended to influence countries purchasing Russian energy or facilitating sanctions evasion. It authorized additional duties of up to 100% on goods imported into the United States from countries meeting specified criteria. The executive order selected that rate but waived its application before the new duties took effect (United States Congress, 2026, Section 113).
The initial statutory criteria distinguish two categories. The first concerns countries among the five largest importers, by volume, of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas during the relevant 12-month period preceding enactment, provided they knowingly make new purchases on or after October 18, 2026. The second concerns the five leading countries facilitating Russian oil-sanctions evasion during that reference period.
The legislation also contains exceptions and procedural requirements. Section 113(d) provides a limited exception concerning natural gas imports where the country's purchases account for less than 15% of Russia's annual natural gas exports during the relevant period and the country has taken significant steps to reduce those imports. Section 113(g) requires advance written justification to Congress explaining the tariff determination and the methodology used to identify the affected country. Subsequent country determinations are addressed separately under Section 113(e).
These conditions prevent a simple equation between purchasing Russian energy and becoming subject to the proposed tariffs. Country eligibility depends on statutory definitions, purchasing conduct, volume rankings, and the relevant exceptions. The October 16 order did not individually designate India, China, or Turkey as countries already subject to the additional 100% duties.
The proposed tariffs also differed from a direct tax on Russian oil purchases. They would have applied to covered merchandise imported into the United States from qualifying countries, potentially including products unrelated to energy. Their suspension consequently removed a prospective commercial penalty extending beyond the petroleum sector, while leaving existing American trade measures unaffected.
1.3 Other Graham Act Sanctions Covered by the Waiver
The October 16 waiver extended beyond customs duties. Section 4(c) suspended the application of specified sanctions and restrictions under Sections 102(a), 102(e), 103–111, and 117 of the Graham Act. These provisions addressed Russian officials, financial institutions, state-controlled enterprises, investment, financial transfers, securities transactions, energy activities, and international financial messaging services (White House, 2026, Section 4(c)).
Several restrictions were intended to limit Russia's access to foreign capital and commercial services. Others concerned American investment in Russia, transactions involving Russian government institutions, and activities supporting specified Russian energy operations. Their implementation depended on the particular statutory provision, including whether a prohibition operated directly or required an individual executive determination.
Section 109 provides an important exception to the general implementation chronology. It prohibited purchases of Russian government sovereign debt by U.S. persons upon enactment on September 18. The October 16 waiver subsequently included this provision. It would be inaccurate to describe every restriction covered by the presidential decision as having been waived before taking legal effect (United States Congress, 2026, Section 109).
The waiver also included Section 111, concerning Russian uranium, and Section 117, governing the termination of sanctions. The latter provision establishes a distinct legal procedure rather than another commercial prohibition. Its inclusion in the waiver does not establish that the conditions for permanent termination were satisfied.
The effect of Section 4(c) was to suspend substantial additional obligations under the Graham Act. It did not establish that every potential sanctions designation had already occurred, nor did it terminate restrictions created under separate American legislation or executive orders.

high_priority_articles.title: A U.S.-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled - PressReader
high_priority_articles.summary: A U.S.-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled  PressReader
high_priority_articles.full_text:
It’s been a year since a ceasefire deal brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump and Arab allies promised to end the war in Gaza, and Israel is still launching deadly strikes on the devastated territory. The agreement halted major military operations, freed all remaining hostages and increased humanitarian access. But it has failed to deliver on promises of a new Palestinian administration aided by international forces, the disarmament of Hamas and an end to Israel’s control over more than half the territory. Almost nothing has been rebuilt. Israel has tied any progress on the other issues to Hamas’ complete disarmament, while the militant group — and the Trump administration — say they should happen simultaneously. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hardened his stance over the summer, openly defying Trump, his most important ally, ahead of Israeli elections later this month.
The wrangling has left Gaza’s 2 million Palestinians in limbo. Most are sheltering in rodent-infested tent camps, the rubble of their former neighborhoods or war-damaged buildings at risk of collapse.
In the Jabaliya area of the northern Gaza Strip, Abdullah Abu Zubaida’s family lives in a makeshift shelter built from the debris of their house.
“When the ceasefire began last October, we expected the war to halt, assassinations to cease, and aid to flow in,” he said. None of that has happened.
For Ne’man Abu Jarad and his family, displaced from Beit Lahia in northern Gaza to Khan Younis in the south, the truce also has brought no clear path home. The family, including five daughters, continues to live in tents.
“The ceasefire is merely nominal, ink on paper,” Abu Jarad said.
Early success raised hopes of ending the war
The 20-point ceasefire agreement, reached after months of negotiations under the Biden and Trump administrations, ended major military operations and led to the return of all the remaining hostages taken in Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack that ignited the war.
Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people that day and abducted 251. Israel responded with massive bombardment and a ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.
After the deal was announced, Trump called for a new era of harmony in the Middle East. “We have a once-in-a-lifetime chance to put the old feuds and bitter hatreds behind us,” he said at a summit marking the deal.
The agreement called for much more
The agreement called for Hamas to hand over power to a committee of Palestinian administrators vetted by the Board of Peace, a new body chaired by Trump and charged with implementing the ceasefire.
The militants officially dissolved their government in July but left the civil ser-*
vice intact and remain the dominant power in the roughly 40% of Gaza not controlled by the Israeli military. Israel has meanwhile barred the new Palestinian administration from entering Gaza via Egypt.
The formation of an International Stabilization Force was announced in February but has yet to materialize. Indonesia, which pledged the largest troop contingent — 8,000 soldiers — put those plans on hold last spring as the world’s focus shifted to the Iran war.
Israel was supposed to withdraw from Gaza but has instead seized more territory, pushing the so-called yellow Line of Control westward toward the Mediterranean Sea. It has also carried out regular strikes on individuals it accused of violating the ceasefire, approaching the yellow line or having taken part in the Oct. 7 attack — strikes that have often killed civilians.
Israeli strikes have killed over 1,400 Palestinians since the ceasefire took effect, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
Sporadic attacks have killed five Israeli soldiers in Gaza in the same period.
More deadlock after Netanyahu defied Trump
In July, Trump announced a deal to disarm Hamas, portraying it as a breakthrough in the long-stalled process.
That deal, an extension of the original ceasefire, called for Hamas to disarm “in a gradual, sequential and time-bound manner” that is “linked to an Israeli withdrawal, in phases.” Hamas confirmed for the first time that it had agreed to disarm, also linking it to Israel halting its strikes and withdrawing from Gaza.
Days later, Netanyahu announced that Israel would not withdraw from any part of Gaza until after Hamas has been completely disarmed, explicitly rejecting the agreement announced by Trump.
The rare instance of friction between the two allies came as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his nationalist base ahead of Oct. 27 elections that could end his nearly unbroken 17-year rule, the longest in Israel’s history.
Netanyahu has come under fire over security and intelligence failures leading up to the Oct. 7 attack, with opponents accusing him of having been soft on Hamas. That gives him little space to make even minor compromises on Gaza, at least until a new government is formed, which could take months.
In the meantime, virtually nothing has been rebuilt in Gaza, Hamas is weakened but still in power, and a return to fighting cannot be ruled out.

high_priority_articles.title: Nigeria, World Bank Move to Tackle AfCFTA Digital Trade Barriers - Nigeria Communications Week
high_priority_articles.summary: Nigeria, World Bank Move to Tackle AfCFTA Digital Trade Barriers  Nigeria Communications Week
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Nigeria is working with the World Bank Group to identify regulatory gaps affecting digital trade as the country seeks to align its domestic policies with the African Continental Free Trade Area’s Digital Trade Protocol.
According to the Nigerian AfCFTA Coordination Office, the initiative will examine how the country’s pending digital economy legislation and planned e-commerce policy can be aligned with continental rules intended to facilitate cross-border digital commerce.
Patience Okala, the office’s national coordinator and chief executive, said the regulatory gap analysis aims to ensure that the protocol, its annexes and Nigeria’s domestic laws and policies operate consistently.
The development comes as African governments seek to reduce regulatory obstacles that prevent businesses from expanding their digital services beyond national borders.
Nigeria has identified Ghana, Egypt, Rwanda, South Africa and Kenya as priority markets for domestic businesses seeking regional expansion. Regulators from the five countries had visited Lagos to examine market-access requirements and identify areas where regulatory processes could be aligned or mutually recognised, Okala said.
Differences in national regulations can complicate cross-border e-commerce, digital payments, electronic transactions and the handling of data.
Businesses operating across multiple African markets may need to navigate different requirements for digital documentation, consumer protection, payment services and regulatory compliance. For smaller companies, these differences can increase the cost of entering new markets and make it harder to scale services across the continent.
In an August 2026 report, the World Bank argued that Africa’s next phase of economic integration depends on reducing trade and regulatory friction and improving connections between national systems. The report identified digital networks, payment infrastructure, customs procedures and services as important components of a more integrated regional market.
The AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol provides a continental framework for addressing some of these challenges. Its implementation, however, depends on countries translating regional commitments into domestic laws, regulations and operational systems.
Nigeria’s proposed National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill is part of that process. The legislation is intended to establish a broader legal framework for the country’s digital economy, while the planned e-commerce policy is expected to support the development of online commercial activity.
The regulatory review will help identify where existing rules and proposed measures need to be aligned with the continental framework.
In related news, Nigeria has also been selected as one of three pilot countries for the Africa Digital Access and Public Infrastructure for Trade initiative, alongside Egypt and Kenya.
The programme, run by the AfCFTA Secretariat and the Tony Blair Institute, aims to advance interoperability between digital systems and support implementation of the Digital Trade Protocol. A team has been inaugurated in Nigeria to work on the initiative, according to Okala.

In an interview with Euronews, Romanian President Nicușor Dan warns that Black Sea security is under growing pressure as drone attacks hit commercial vessels off Romania and Bulgaria.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan has said the Black Sea would only become safe after Russia’s war in Ukraine ends, as he called for greater NATO oversight in the region following drone strikes on commercial vessels in an interview with Euronews.
“I’m very optimistic that we’ll have the support and the capabilities in order to be better protected, because it’s an important economic question for Ukraine and for the whole region,” he said on the sidelines of an EU summit in Brussels held Friday.
The Romanian leader said frequent drone incursions into his country’s territory had begun roughly a year and a half ago, and that Bucharest had been “not prepared”. The country now faces a similar lack of preparedness to its east, Dan said.
“At the Black Sea, we are in the same situation,” he said, adding: “We have to protect the water under our territory.”
He also expressed confidence in continued support from US President Donald Trump, both for security in the Black Sea and for Romania’s position within the NATO military alliance.
“On defence, I think it’s a mutual benefit between us because we have an excellent position to project force towards other parts of the world,” Dan said.
The confidence comes amid bellicose statements from US President Donald Trump regarding Ukrainian and European security, such as troop cuts and a force posture review.
The president was in the Belgian capital for a quarterly summit attended by EU heads of state to discuss support for Ukraine, the bloc’s long-term budget and its growing trade deficit with China.
However, the increasingly hostile security situation in the Black Sea pushed the Romanian leader and his Bulgarian counterpart, Prime Minister Rumen Radev, to bring security threats higher up the agenda.
Dan told reporters after the summit that France had pledged “necessary equipment” and to “better understand our specific requirements in the Black Sea”.
“There are always new challenges, but fortunately, Romania has allies,” he said.
The escalating situation also prompted a meeting between the two leaders and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte to discuss stronger support. Bulgaria requested combat aircraft and anti-drone systems during the talks.
Rutte said afterwards that NATO would continue to strengthen its posture along the eastern flank, including by expanding its counter-drone capabilities.
“NATO will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed,” he said in a statement on the social media platform X.
Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian ports along the Black Sea and the Danube River, leaving the war-torn country dependent on alternative routes to sell its grain to African and Middle Eastern markets.
However, this has exposed Europe’s shipping lanes to attacks.
Drones have damaged commercial vessels in the Black Sea off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania for three consecutive days leading up to the meeting in Brussels, as well as during the previous week. At least one vessel sank after being attacked by drones last week, killing two seafarers.
Neither Sofia nor Bucharest has definitively blamed Russia for the attacks. However, Radev told reporters earlier in the week that “logic” would suggest the Kremlin stood to benefit from the deadly incursions.
“The problem is that we cannot prove it,” he said.
Investigations into all the incidents are ongoing.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a press conference after meeting European leaders on Thursday that “you do not need a ground war for an invasion to occur”.
He added that Russia was testing Europe’s response to the attacks, referring to incidents in the Black Sea as well as an explosive-laden drone found at an airport in Leipzig.
“Violating another country's airspace is already an incursion,” Zelenskyy said.
“We have seen drones cross airspace and borders in Romania, Poland and Germany. A corresponding drone was found in Germany, by the way. Moldova and Bulgaria have also been affected. A great deal is happening today.”
Zelenskyy and other senior Ukrainian officials have publicly blamed Russia for some of these incidents, most notably a deadly drone attack that struck a vessel carrying Ukrainian grain off the Bulgarian coast.

high_priority_articles.summary: Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means  Al JazeeraIran-aligned Houthis launch deadly attack on Yemeni presidential palace in escalating campaign against Saudi Arabia  CNNMissiles hit Aden airport as Saudi-led coalition intercepts missile headed for Yanbu  ReutersIran war updates: Five killed, 16 hurt in Houthi attack on palace in Aden  Al JazeeraHouthi Missiles Strike Government Headquarters in Yemen  The New York Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have fired missiles at the presidential palace in the southern Yemeni city of Aden, killing five people and wounding 16, on Thursday.
On Friday, two missiles landed on the grounds of Aden International Airport as a passenger plane prepared to take off for Cairo.
Recommended Stories
After the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014, the internationally recognised government of Yemen decamped to Aden with the backing of a Saudi-led coalition of Arab countries.
The latest attacks come as Yemen’s war, largely frozen under a 2022 truce, has reignited and become another front in the wider regional conflict involving Iran.
So what has happened in Aden, and why does it matter?
Here’s what you need to know:
What happened at Maashiq Palace?
The Houthis hit the Al-Maashiq Presidential Palace with five missiles, according to Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani.
Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said the dead and wounded included guards and civilian employees.
The government said Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and other officials were safe, but two of his bodyguards had been killed.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had struck what he called the “Saudi military operations headquarters” in Aden.
What happened at the airport?
On Friday, two missiles landed on the airport’s grounds, according to the Aden Security Department, which blamed the Houthis. It said it was the second attack on the facility in less than a week.
Yemenia Flight 612 to Cairo was preparing for takeoff. Al-Eryani said the missiles landed about 500 metres (1,600ft) from the aircraft. No casualties were reported.
Al-Eryani called the strike “a direct threat to the lives of passengers and aviation crews”.
The Houthi-run Saba agency claimed the group was targeting a military headquarters and weapons depots inside Badr Camp, a military site next to the airport.
Why are attacks on Aden significant?
Aden is the interim capital of Yemen.
The government moved there after the Houthis took control of the capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government.
The al-Maashiq Palace is the internationally recognised government’s headquarters and its seat of power.
The Houthis currently control much of the country’s north and west. Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi coalition supporting the government had largely ended following a 2022 ceasefire.
But in September, the Houthis launched a lightning offensive along the Red Sea coast, seizing territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Nearly two weeks ago, government forces launched a counteroffensive dubbed “Operation Dawn of Yemen” with Saudi air support, but have so far failed to reverse those gains.
Saree said the Houthi attacks on Aden were part of the group’s declared policy of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”.
The city has been hit before.
In December 2020, an attack on Aden airport as a new cabinet arrived from Saudi Arabia killed at least 22 people.
A second attack hit the palace where ministers had been taken to safety. The coalition blamed the Houthis, who denied responsibility.
What reaction has there been?
On Thursday, Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, blamed Iran for having “encouraged” the escalation.
He said the Iran-backed Houthis had rejected an offer to meet for talks in Oman when the latest round of hostilities began.
Tehran denied the claim on Friday. “The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.
Baghaei said Iran “has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities”, offering again to mediate.
Canada’s embassy in Saudi Arabia condemned the palace attack and called for “an immediate de-escalation of hostilities”.
“We stand in solidarity with the internationally recognised Government of Yemen and the Yemeni people,” the Canadian embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a post on X.
On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council condemned escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including those affecting civil aviation and energy infrastructure.
The governing council of the UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization also condemned recent attacks on civilian airports and aircraft in Saudi Arabia.
On October 9, Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, told the UNSC the country had slid back into “full-scale war”.
What is happening in the wider conflict?
Fighting resumed in July, ending a 2022 truce.
Last month, the Houthis took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most important waterways. Since the Strait of Hormuz was closed by Iran in March amid US strikes, Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on sending oil exports to the Red Sea via its East-West pipeline instead. The Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ships there earlier in the year.
On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, president of the Presidential Leadership Council, announced Operation Dawn of Yemen to retake Houthi-held territory, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition said 100 fighter jets took part, its first acknowledgement since 2022 that it had resumed air attacks on the Houthis.
The Houthis, in turn, have repeatedly fired missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.
On Friday, the coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile headed for Yanbu, a Red Sea oil hub which Saudi Arabia has been using to export crude.
On the ground, fighting has intensified in Taiz governorate, where the Houthis have been holding the city of Taiz under siege, and which borders the Red Sea. State-run Saba media outlet, citing the Taiz Axis military command, reported that 168 Houthi fighters had been killed and 210 wounded there.
In Houthi-held areas, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what it called “Saudi aggression” since September 3.
Early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported attacks east of Saada, with the coalition saying it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers there.

high_priority_articles.title: Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia - Al Jazeera
high_priority_articles.summary: Egypt’s Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia  Al JazeeraEgypt's Sisi seeks parliament's backing to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked  ReutersEgypt's Sissi says he'll defend Saudi Arabia, if asked  DW.comEgypt said to mull supporting defense of Saudi Arabia in face of Houthi attacks  The Times of IsraelEgypt prepared to defend Saudi Arabia after deadly Houthi airport attack  New York Post
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called for an emergency parliamentary session to authorise him to approve any requests from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance, if Riyadh were to ask.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy on Saturday, el-Sisi emphasised Cairo’s readiness to back the kingdom.
Egypt will “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia “in accordance with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and the directives of the Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman”, he said.
“I know that this matter requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I hope that parliament will convene in an emergency session to give us this authorisation, if it is requested of us,” he said.
“I am not speaking in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone. I am speaking only for defence.”
Attacks on Saudi Arabia
The request follows a barrage of attacks on the kingdom from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, including airports and oil facilities.
Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of the capital, Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport earlier this month killed 14 people and wounded more than 300. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Dammam, Abha, Jazan and Najran.
Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government launched a full-scale military campaign against the Houthis this month to recapture territory seized by them.
El-Sisi had backed Saudi calls for secure and unhindered navigation in the Red Sea in a meeting with the Saudi Crown Prince, known as MBS, in Cairo last month.
A statement from the Egyptian presidency then said that “the security of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”.
Red Sea security
That meeting came just days after the Houthis seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, gaining significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia already has a defence pact with Pakistan and Turkiye, known as the Mecca Alliance for Defence, which was signed in August.
Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under the pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
Analysts say Riyadh is looking for help to protect the kingdom and Red Sea shipping and that Egypt, whose Suez Canal revenue depends on the same traffic, is an obvious partner.
They say Egypt is eager to prevent Iran and its allies from imposing control over the region, especially over maritime traffic in the Red Sea, given the direct repercussions for the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging Houthi attacks against the kingdom, a claim Tehran rejects. Iran has offered assistance to halt the conflict between the two sides.
Sisi’s future
Speaking to recruits at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital on Saturday, el-Sisi also confirmed that he would not seek to extend his presidency beyond 2030, in line with the Egyptian constitution.
“The period leading up to 2030 will be the end of my term as president of the state, if I am still alive,” he said.
He added that his decision is “completely settled” and there will be “no discussion” about it.
Egypt’s constitution was updated in 2019 to increase term length to six years from four, and to allow el-Sisi to run for another six-year term in 2023. That means his term is due to expire in 2030, and he is not allowed to run again.
He said the Egyptian constitution “would not be touched”.
