high_priority_articles.title: ‘Sleepwalking into Putin’s trap’: How Russia is waiting at the gates of Europe - The i Paper
high_priority_articles.summary: ‘Sleepwalking into Putin’s trap’: How Russia is waiting at the gates of Europe  The i PaperNATO’s Top Commander Lays Out Plan to Thwart a Russian Attack on the Alliance  WSJNATO Details Plan to Shield Ukraine’s European Allies From Russia  The New York TimesRussia is at war with Nato ‘today’, says former top military commander  The IndependentNATO Has a Plan to Fend Off Russia. Now It Needs the Will  Bloomberg.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Nato’s top commander issued a stark warning this week, saying that his troops will destroy “anything and everything” involved if a country was “foolish enough” to launch an attack on its territory.
“If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight,” US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich told the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday. “We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be.”
Grynkewich’s blunt remarks came at a time of escalating tensions between Europe and Russia, with concerns that Moscow is preparing to expand its aggression beyond Ukraine, even by staging a limited military incursion to test Nato’s resolve.
On the front lines, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have for years warned of Moscow’s ambitions. But as the Kremlin escalates its aggression, and with Nato failing to deter it, the Baltics are increasingly worried Europe could be stumbling into a trap.
Russia’s brutal legacy in the Baltics
Artis Pabriks, a former defence minister and deputy prime minister of Latvia, told The i Paper that Russia has for years been using “strategic communications or cognitive warfare” within Nato to “depict the Baltic countries as something to which Russia might have more rights than it usually could have”.
Like much of Eastern Europe, the Baltic states endured decades of brutal Soviet occupation, until the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, an event Vladimir Putin has described as “the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the century”. The Russian president has made reasserting Moscow’s dominance over former Soviet republics a core objective for his rule.
And Putin’s aims go beyond the control of foreign affairs and into direct influence over aspects of the internal policies of post-Soviet states, according to the Institute for the Study of War in Washington DC, which said that the Kremlin sees these countries as rightful parts of its sphere of influence.
“The Kremlin is working to split Nato,” said Edward Lucas, founder of the Baltic International Security Centre. “Specifically separating the Baltics and others including Poland from the rest of Europe, to deprive them of the protections of Nato and EU membership.”
The Baltics’ location bordering Russia means that they are more exposed than most Nato countries, and Nato’s reluctance so far to strongly confront Russia appears to be increasing the likelihood of greater aggression from Moscow.
“What worries many of us in the Baltic region is that we are sleepwalking into such a trap,” warned Pabriks.
The Baltic states are small: Estonia has a population of just 1.33 million, Latvia 1.9 million and Lithuania 2.79 million. Lithuania is also located between Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad and its ally Belarus, with the Suwałki Gap to the south. This strategic 40-mile corridor links Kaliningrad to the rest of Russia via Belarus. In the event of a conflict, closure of the gap would cut off the three countries from land reinforcements.
Moscow preparing ‘something symbolic’
While an outright invasion has largely been dismissed, with Russia still tied down in Ukraine, Putin could still see the benefit of targeting the region as a way to undermine Nato.
The Baltics have “long been a focus of Russian military planning, information operations, cyber activities and other forms of hybrid pressure”, said Melita Phachulia of the Stockholm Centre for Research and Innovation Security.
And Moscow has plenty of options, she added. “A more likely scenario would be Russia testing Nato’s cohesion through limited or ambiguous actions that remain below the threshold of conventional war,” Phachulia said, adding that this might include more actions like the sabotage of undersea cables, GPS jamming, drone incursions or the “weaponisation” of migration.
Lithuania’s president, Gitanas Nausėda, said in July that Russia was planning potential attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltics or Poland, while Latvian intelligence has said that Putin was considering more hybrid attacks designed to “send a signal: stop supporting Ukraine, or you will have your own problems”.
According to Lucas: “Russia could do something symbolic, and that’s what we’re seeing at the moment: Russian testing, attacking our decision-making. And that is our weak point… That’s a problem in Brussels, chiefly Berlin, London, Paris, and of course Washington DC.”
Could Russia weaponise an ‘internal threat’?
There are fears, however, that Nato’s reluctance to confront such incidents could encourage Putin to try a small-scale incursion. Reports suggested that CIA director John Ratcliffe flew to Moscow in August to try to warn Russia against further escalations, especially in the Baltics.
“It’s not necessarily that Putin plans to occupy Estonia or Latvia or Lithuania,” said Pabriks. “But for him, it’s important to have a case where he can show that Nato doesn’t react properly and it’s an empty shell. He could do something against some Nato member country which is close to their border, say to take 5 sq km….We give up our freedoms by centimetres and metres and kilometres. And one day we wake up and we are under their boot.”
In 2021, leaked documents from the Russian presidential administration revealed it was planning to maintain influence in the Baltics by funding pro-Russian groups.
Estonia and Latvia have the largest number of ethnic Russians in the EU as a proportion of their populations, and Moscow has tried to weaponise Russian speakers in the Baltics as part of efforts to complicate relations with their Western partners. Russia has also used this playbook elsewhere, including in Ukraine.
In the Baltics, anonymous Telegram channels and low-level agitation has worked to spread discontent over issues including campaigns to remove Soviet-era monuments and Latvia’s move to reduce Russian-language instructions in schools. However, there is little sign of serious discontent.
“Since 1991, Russia has never in any seriousness tried to foment separatism in the Baltic,” said Donatas Kupčiūnas, Baltic fellow at Cambridge University’s Centre for Geopolitics, with Moscow’s policies to minorities abroad “subsumed under broader strategic considerations”. He added that even Latvia’s recent language measures prompted “only lukewarm protests from Russia, because it has bigger problems to deal with”.
Meanwhile in Estonia, attachment to the Russian language has gone hand in hand with increased loyalty to Estonia, according to Institut Montaigne, a Paris-based think-tank. “There’s no sort of ‘minority’ in the Baltic hankering to be liberated from local rule and put under under rule of Moscow,” said Lucas.
‘We will respond with all the force we can find’
“Vulnerability should not be confused with weakness,” said Phachulia.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have invested heavily in defence and resilience, taking a whole-of-society approach with conscription and massive reserve military forces. All are outsized defence spenders, at around 5 per cent of GDP, while a Baltic Defence Line of fortifications, bunkers and anti-tank obstacles now winds along their borders with Russia and Belarus.
The presence of “trip-wire” troops from across Nato – a UK-led battlegroup in Estonia, and another each in Latvia and Lithuania – as well as air policing and reinforced regional defence plans, further seek to underscore that “any attack on the Baltics is not an attack on the Baltics – it’s an attack on Nato”, said Lucas.
Right now, Russia knows it cannot win a war against Nato. However, by escalating sub-threshold attacks in places like the Baltics, it is hoping that it may not need to.
The Baltics have warned Nato allies that if it cannot establish deterrence or punish Russia for hostile actions, Putin will grow bolder. “Russia is not our problem,” Pabriks said, ironically. “Our problem is our allies, which for decades have not been listening to what we have been telling them. Russia is escalating, and it is escalating because the West did not choose to respond.”
“Pull yourselves together and start to act, because we all are in danger with this,” he said of Nato.

high_priority_articles.title: India’s goods trade deficit widens - Business Recorder
high_priority_articles.summary: India’s goods trade deficit widens  Business Recorder
high_priority_articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: India’s merchandise trade deficit widened to USD30.21 billion in September as the rise in imports outpaced that in exports, though a rise in outbound shipments and trade deals could narrow the balance over coming months.
The trade gap has widened as Asia’s third-largest economy grapples with a prolonged Iran war that has made energy costlier, hurt shipments to the Middle East and battered markets.
India raised interest rates earlier this month and announced a raft of measures to support the rupee. India’s trade deficit stood at USD26.86 billion in August.
Merchandise exports rose to USD44.40 billion in September from USD43.81 billion in the previous month, while imports increased to USD74.61 billion from USD70.67 billion. Export growth was broad-based, reflecting strength across sectors including petroleum products, meat, dairy, poultry, electronic goods, handicrafts, and engineering goods, Trade Secretary Rajesh Agrawal told reporters.
India is seeking to diversify its export markets, with a trade deal with New Zealand set to take effect next week and its pact with the UK already in force, while a broader agreement with the EU is moving towards implementation.
Agrawal said negotiations with the US were moving in the “right direction,” with legal work underway. “We anticipate concluding and signing the trade deal at the earliest possible time,” Agrawal said, adding that India was seeking preferential market access and greater tariff stability under the proposed agreement.
Ties with the US have been rocky this past year over issues including President Donald Trump’s repeated claim of brokering an India-Pakistan ceasefire and a US military attack on a ship off Oman that killed three Indian seafarers.
The US remained the top destination for Indian exports, with goods shipments rising to USD50.81 billion in April-September from USD45.82 billion a year earlier.
India’s services exports stood at USD36.35 billion in September, and imports at USD19.44 billion, trade ministry estimates showed. Overall goods and services exports rose 13.84 percent year-on-year to USD476.20 billion in April-September from a year earlier, while imports increased 15.68 percent to USD551.13 billion, data showed.

high_priority_articles.title: US tariff waiver on Russian crude a comforting relief, but trade uncertainties persist: CareEdge Chief Economist Rajani Sinha - India's News.Net
high_priority_articles.summary: US tariff waiver on Russian crude a comforting relief, but trade uncertainties persist: CareEdge Chief Economist Rajani Sinha  India's News.Net
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 17(ANI): In the high-stakes arena of global energy politics, Washington's decision to pull back on its aggressive tariff threats has handed India crucial macroeconomic breathing room, according Rajani Sinha.
Sinha, Chief Economist at CareEdge, told ANI on Saturday that while the tariff waiver provides comforting relief, India must remain cautious amid uncertainties in global trade dynamics.
Addressing the threat of steep US tariffs, Sinha noted that markets viewed the rhetoric primarily as a negotiating technique rather than an immediate structural threat.
'Up to 100% tariff that the US had threatened India with, we were not much concerned about it,' Sinha said. 'We viewed that more as a negotiating technique by the US'.
However, she cautioned that the reprieve might be temporary, underscoring the importance of securing a comprehensive bilateral trade deal with Washington.
Sinha highlighted that the waiver benefits the United States just as much as its trading partners, given Washington's own energy security concerns and widening diesel crack spreads.
With global oil markets remaining volatile, she pointed out that India's refined petroleum products are vital for helping the US curb domestic inflation.
On the energy front, Sinha noted that while Russia has become a critical source supplying over 30 per cent of India's crude imports, the historical discounting advantage has significantly narrowed.
Russian crude currently trades at around $117 per barrel compared to Brent spot prices near $120.
'The benefit that India enjoyed in terms of lower Russian oil, that has really, I would say, dwindled,' Sinha remarked, adding that Russian imports now serve primarily to secure steady, reliable energy availability rather than steep price discounts.
Despite high crude prices, India's macroeconomic buffers remain resilient.
Sinha projected the current account deficit (CAD) to stay comfortably between 0.8 per cent and 1.2 per cent of GDP, supported by robust double-digit growth in merchandise and services exports.
Headline inflation is expected to average around 5 per cent for the fiscal year, though persistent crude prices above $100 per barrel could pose upside risks if passed on to consumers.
On the currency front, she attributed recent rupee depreciation primarily to adverse global sentiment and foreign capital flows rather than weak domestic fundamentals.
Turning to the fiscal deficit, Sinha noted that healthy direct and indirect tax collections will provide a substantial cushion.
Concluding with the government's disinvestment pipeline, she addressed market debates regarding the IDBI Bank stake sale.
Backing the move, Sinha stressed that the transaction represents a positive step toward meeting budgetary targets and reducing the state's footprint in the commercial sector.
'I do not see any concern for the banking sector,' Sinha affirmed, noting that India's banking health and robust NPA metrics remain well-positioned.
The move comes after US President Donald Trump waived the sanctions provisions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which could have imposed tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, including India and China. Trump invoked Section 115 of the Act, citing US national interests, amid a diesel supply deal with Russia.
India had conveyed its concerns to Washington over the legislation, with the Ministry of External Affairs on Wednesday, reiterating New Delhi's position that stability in global energy markets must be maintained. (ANI)

high_priority_articles.title: Non-tariff barriers biggest hurdle in India-China trade: Sitharaman - The New Indian Express
high_priority_articles.summary: Non-tariff barriers biggest hurdle in India-China trade: Sitharaman  The New Indian Express
high_priority_articles.full_text:
China’s restrictions on Indian exports have emerged as the biggest obstacle to bilateral trade, widening India’s trade deficit despite an improvement in diplomatic relations between the two countries in recent times, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Friday.
During her interaction with the Atlantic Council on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok, Sitharaman flagged China’s extensive use of non-tariff barriers, which she said had prevented Indian exporters from accessing the Chinese market despite significant opportunities.
“I would think a decade has gone, consistently putting up a case for market access for Indian products. But non-tariff barriers have been very strong and China uses non-tariff barriers unhesitatingly, whether it is in the name of phytosanitary measures or any other for which due investigations can happen. Both sides can resolve the issues by talks. But no progress has been made. So, non-tariff barriers are the biggest hurdle in the trade between India and China,” the minister said.
India has recently relaxed Press Note 3 norms, which had restricted Chinese entities from making foreign direct investment in India through the automatic route. However, the widening trade gap remains a key concern, with imports from China continuing to far exceed exports.
According to the latest government data, India’s imports from China rose nearly 28% to $80.35 billion during April-September this year, while exports stood at $11.41 billion.
India’s trade deficit with China more than doubled to $112 billion in FY26 from $52.7 billion in FY16.
“The trade imbalance is something which we have been talking with China now for several years; we are denied market access even for those goods for which there are immense market opportunities in China,” Sitharaman said.
She said the two countries could address concerns over non-tariff measures through dialogue and investigations, but there had been little progress. New Delhi, meanwhile, had refrained from imposing retaliatory non-tariff restrictions or countervailing duties on Chinese goods.
On the India-US trade negotiations, Sitharaman expressed hope that the agreement would be concluded soon.
“I hope in the interest of global trade and in the interest of trade between the two partners India and US the trade agreement gets concluded at the earliest,” she said.

high_priority_articles.title: Non-Tariff Barriers Biggest Hurdle in India-China Trade: Nirmala Sitharaman - Open Magazine
high_priority_articles.summary: Non-Tariff Barriers Biggest Hurdle in India-China Trade: Nirmala Sitharaman  Open Magazine
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Non-tariff barriers remain the biggest obstacle to trade between India and China, with restricted market access for Indian goods contributing to a widening trade imbalance, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Friday.
Speaking at an interactive session with Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council on India’s Economic Edge, held on the sidelines of the World Bank-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, Sitharaman said India had repeatedly raised concerns over the barriers faced by its products in the Chinese market but had seen limited progress.
“So non-tariff barriers are the biggest hurdle in the trade between India and China,” she said, adding that the trade imbalance continued to grow despite years of engagement between the two countries.
Sitharaman said Indian products faced restrictions even in sectors where the country was globally competitive and where demand in China offered significant opportunities.
“We are global leaders in generic drugs, bovine meat, vegetables and perishables and very many such goods which have huge potential in China,” she said.
She alleged that China used measures such as phytosanitary requirements to restrict market access, arguing that these issues could be addressed through investigations and bilateral discussions.
INDIA FAVOURS DIALOGUE OVER RETALIATORY TARIFFS
Sitharaman said India had chosen to pursue discussions rather than respond to trade barriers with countervailing duties or similar restrictions.
She contrasted India's approach with that of countries that impose tariffs to address what they consider unsustainable trade imbalances.
“That approach we have never taken,” she said, adding that negotiations could be slow but remained India's preferred way of resolving trade disputes.
The remarks highlight a longstanding challenge in India-China economic relations: despite substantial bilateral commerce, the trade balance is heavily tilted towards China. India has repeatedly sought greater access for its exports while raising concerns about dependence on Chinese imports.
Non-tariff barriers include regulatory requirements, product standards, licensing procedures and other restrictions that can affect the movement of goods across borders, even when tariffs are not the principal obstacle.
INDIA-US TRADE AGREEMENT ALSO IN FOCUS
Beyond China, Sitharaman expressed hope that India and the United States would conclude their proposed trade agreement at the earliest opportunity.
She referred to recent remarks by India's commerce minister indicating that both sides wanted to move towards signing the agreement soon.
“I hope, in the interest of global trade and in the interest of trade between the two partners, India and US, the trade agreement gets concluded at the earliest,” she said.
India has been pursuing trade agreements with several partners as part of its efforts to expand export opportunities, improve market access and diversify economic relationships.
Sitharaman reiterated India's commitment to multilateralism while highlighting its trade engagements with the United Arab Emirates, Australia, Canada and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) bloc, alongside negotiations with the US.
Her comments come as governments worldwide reassess trade relationships amid tariff disputes, supply-chain concerns and efforts to secure more favourable terms for domestic industries.

Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia Defy Difference in Military Power
By Gerry Doyle (Bloomberg) — The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are demonstrating the limits of the kingdom’s military prowess — despite defense spending that far outstrips that of its regional neighbors.
Missiles and drones fired by the Iran-backed group from Yemen have wreaked havoc in Saudi Arabia in recent days, killing at least 18 people and forcing the closure of the country’s main international airport in Riyadh. The Houthis are showing no sign of scaling back their campaign, targeting several Saudi Arabian cities in an assault this week that’s continued into Thursday.
Saudi Arabia allocated between $64 billion and $96 billion this year for defense, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Economics. The upper end is more than twice as much as Israel, the next biggest Middle East spender.
Video Muted
The kingdom operates Raytheon Co. Patriot missile batteries with the latest Lockheed Martin Corp. PAC-3 interceptors, flies hundreds of Boeing Co. F-15 fighters customized for its air force, and is the only Gulf country with mid-air refueling aircraft.
One reason the Houthis have been able to cause such destruction with less advanced equipment is Saudi Arabia’s size, which complicates defense efforts.The kingdom covers more than 2.1 million square kilometers (830,000 square miles), with many strategic targets to protect, from oil infrastructure to air bases to several large cities.
Defending against ballistic missiles is complex when protecting a single target, let alone sites sprinkled across a vast country. Thousands of Iranian strikes across the Arabian peninsula during the initial phase of the US and Israeli war on the Islamic Republic were largely thwarted by missile defenses, but even a 90% success rate can mean massive damage on the ground.
Saudi Arabia’s military is also still in the process of modernizing and remains heavily reliant on the US for military intelligence.
The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment.
The most recent rounds of Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have tended to involve a mix of weapons that further complicate defensive efforts: small drones, low-flying, cheap cruise missiles and ballistic missiles.
In addition, the Houthis are a nimble, rapidly evolving opponent backed by Iran, capable of building and deploying missiles and drones that can challenge even advanced defense systems. Years of fighting in Yemen mean the group is battle hardened, resisting protracted military efforts to dislodge or contain them.
“The Houthis are partly beneficiaries of good fortune, but they seem remarkably adaptive,” said Ankit Panda, Stanton Senior Fellow in the Nuclear Policy Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “A determined attacker armed with missiles is still difficult to deal with.”
The Houthi arsenal has now evolved to the point where the group can manufacture relatively precise drones and ballistic missiles — some of which rely on parts from Chinese companies. Those munitions might cost thousands, or hundreds of thousands of dollars, far cheaper than the multimillion-dollar air defense interceptors used to stop them.
That means even a successfully intercepted attack imposes further costs on Saudi Arabia, and makes it more vulnerable to future strikes.
Defensive weapons such as the Iranian-made 358 surface-to-air missiles — which can loiter at high altitudes and strike subsonic aircraft — make the skies over Yemen dangerous too.
Another issue, said Bloomberg Economics defense lead Becca Wasser, is that Patriot air defense batteries are directional. They do not cover a 360-degree area, so if radars and launchers were positioned to intercept Iranian fire, they may not have been able to easily shoot down Houthi missiles, she said.
Air and missile capabilities have improved as part of Saudi Arabia’s modernization efforts, Wasser said. Although pilots learned considerably from the long Yemen air war, their aircraft remain largely reliant on the US for targeting data, in particular.
The situation has improved since Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman began a reform agenda, alongside “real-life experience in its first war against Yemen,” Wasser said. “But modernization is slow and confined to pockets of bright spots rather than upskilling across the force.”
Although Riyadh has a fleet of more than 200 F-15 jets — almost as many as the US Air Force — it was unable to use them decisively in more than a decade of bombing the Houthis. Saudi Arabia went to war with the militant group in 2015 after it took control of the Yemeni capital, Saana, though fighting receded between a 2022 truce and the recent flare up.
“Equipment and funding do not win wars,” said Wolf-Christian Paes, a senior fellow for armed conflict at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. “Training, motivation and leadership do.”
US influence in the Middle East after 1990 — when Washington intervened after Iraq invaded Kuwait — prompted many countries in the region to rely on US firepower rather than fully develop their own capabilities.
Saudi Arabia was not immune to this “protection curse,” said David Roberts, a reader in international security and Middle East studies at King’s College London.
US struggles in Afghanistan, and incidents like the 2019 Houthi drone attack against oil facilities in Abqaiq, in the east of Saudi Arabia, punctured the image that “Uncle Sam would basically detect and protect,” Roberts said.
US President Donald Trump has so far opted against intervening directly in the current conflict. In a post on Truth Social on Tuesday he said the Houthis were “behaving very badly,” without specifying what action the US could take.
Saudi Oil Minister Prince Abdul Aziz Bin Salman said this week that “the events of recent weeks are serious,” adding that the kingdom’s response “must be equally serious, while remaining focused on the decades ahead.”
The Houthis began threatening shipping in the Red Sea after the start of the war in Gaza, which prompted the US to briefly intervene, launching more than 1,000 strikes over three months. But hunting down hidden, mobile launchers and shutting down buried production facilities is difficult, especially in the rugged terrain in which the Houthis operate. The operation ended with a ceasefire.
The Houthis show “there are very clear limits what an air campaign can do,” said April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Former US Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin, speaking at the Warsaw Defense Forum on Monday, said Saudi Arabia would most likely need help from friendly nations to counter the Houthi threat.
“There will be a concerted effort to get the Houthi thing under control,” he said. “But it won’t be easy. They are much more resilient than most people recognize.”
The conflicts in Iran and Ukraine have shown how the power of ballistic missiles, particularly those with a range of 1,000 kilometers or more, mean even countries whose millitaries are relatively weak can cause problems for more powerful adversaries.
The Houthis’ strike arsenal includes indigenously produced Quds-1 cruise missiles, which have a reach of about 750 kilometers, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Its homegrown ballistic arsenal is larger, with Burkan-1, -2, and -3 designs, which can fly 600 kilometers, 850 kilometers and 1,200 kilometers, respectively, giving the militants the range to hit nearly any site in Saudi Arabia.
Riyadh’s struggles to extinguish the Houthi threat and defend against counterattacks reflects the difficulty of a task many others have failed at too.

high_priority_articles.title: Tanzania Advances Southern Railway Plan with Egypt’s Arab Contractors - The Chanzo
high_priority_articles.summary: Tanzania Advances Southern Railway Plan with Egypt’s Arab Contractors  The Chanzo
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Dar es Salaam — Tanzania has taken a step towards developing a railway linking Mtwara Port with mineral-rich southern regions and Mbamba Bay on Lake Nyasa after Tanzania Railways Corporation (TRC) signed an agreement with Egypt’s state-owned construction company, Arab Contractors, to conduct preliminary studies and a feasibility assessment.
The proposed Southern Corridor Railway Line, estimated at approximately 1,000 kilometres, aims to facilitate the transportation of minerals, agricultural produce and industrial goods while improving access to regional markets. A branch is also planned to serve the Mchuchuma coal and Liganga iron ore projects.
Speaking during the signing ceremony, Friday, October 16, 2026, TRC Director General Machibya Shiwa said the agreement establishes a framework for technical and financial studies, including an assessment of possible financing options for the project.
“Under the agreement, Arab Contractors will undertake preliminary studies at its own cost and is expected to submit an initial report within three months,” said Machibya, “TRC will provide technical information, coordinate relevant institutions and review the findings.”
Transport Minister Professor Makame Mbarawa said the railway could unlock economic opportunities in southern Tanzania by connecting agricultural production areas, mineral deposits and industrial projects with Mtwara Port.
READ MORE: Tanzania, Burundi Kick Off Landmark Standard Gauge Railway Project
He directed both parties to establish a work plan defining responsibilities, expected results and implementation timelines. He also stressed that the studies must examine actual freight demand, construction costs, financing options and the long-term sustainability of railway operations.
“The agreements being signed today constitute a preparatory step for this important project,” Mbarawa said, adding that the studies should establish transport requirements, economic benefits and possible financing arrangements.
Reviving the Mtwara Development Corridor
The proposal also revives ambitions associated with the Mtwara Development Corridor, a regional initiative advanced by Southern African Development Community (SADC) leaders in 2004 to promote trade and investment among Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique and Zambia.
The initiative envisaged coordinated infrastructure development, including roads, railways, ports, bridges, energy networks and telecommunications, to connect previously underserved areas with regional and international markets.
Proposed projects included the Unity Bridge across the Ruvuma River between Tanzania and Mozambique, improved transport infrastructure connections between Mtwara and Mbamba Bay, and transport links across Lake Nyasa. Energy cooperation and the development of Mchuchuma’s coal reserves were also identified as potential drivers of regional growth.
READ MORE: AfDB Approves Over $600m for 650-Kilometre Tanzania, Burundi Rail Infrastructure
More than two decades later, the Southern Corridor Railway could help realise part of that vision. Yet its regional benefits will depend on complementary investments and cooperation with neighbouring countries.
A connection to Mbamba Bay could facilitate onward transportation towards Malawi and Mozambique, while Mtwara Port could offer regional businesses another gateway to international markets.
Building on railway expansion
The proposed southern line would complement Tanzania’s broader railway development programme, including the Standard Gauge Railway network connecting central Tanzania with destinations such as Mwanza and Kigoma.
While those investments strengthen transport along the country’s central axis, the Southern Corridor Railway would focus on connecting southern production centres with the coast and neighbouring markets.
Arab Contractors brings experience from major infrastructure projects in Tanzania, having participated in the consortium involved in implementing the 2,115-megawatt Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project. However, its current agreement concerns feasibility studies and does not constitute a construction contract.
Beyond minerals, improved railway access could support agricultural trade, industrial investment, employment and tourism. The corridor encompasses attractions including Lake Nyasa, the Kitulo Plateau, Selous Game Reserve, Indian Ocean beaches and marine parks.
Nevertheless, these benefits will require complementary investment, local skills development, environmental protection and meaningful community participation.

high_priority_articles.title: Railway tracks return to Arish after decades as Sinai rail project advances - Urban & Transport - Egypt - Ahram Online
high_priority_articles.summary: Railway tracks return to Arish after decades as Sinai rail project advances - Urban & Transport - Egypt  Ahram Online
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Railway tracks have reached Arish for the first time since 1967, local media reported, marking a long-awaited step toward reconnecting the North Sinai city to Egypt’s national railway network.
The arrival advances the Sinai railway project, a roughly 500-kilometre route linking Fardan, East Port Said, Bir Al-Abd, Arish and Taba to serve passengers, industry and trade across the peninsula.
Sinai News Network published footage late Friday, credited to journalist Ahmed Abu Deraa, showing rails laid on concrete sleepers and describing their arrival as the first since 1967.
The footage drew celebratory reactions on social media, with users welcoming the railway’s return and expressing pride in development efforts across Sinai.
The construction marks a new chapter for Arish, where the railway once carried passengers and goods across northern Sinai before the June 1967 war cut its connection to Egypt’s national network.
In a September statement, the Ministry of Transport said 11 Egyptian companies were carrying out earthworks on the 83-kilometer Bir Al-Abd–Arish section, along with the construction of seven stations.
These include Al-Sadat, Al-Teloul, Shuhadaa Al-Rawda, Salt Factory, Al-Masaeed, Sinai–Central Arish, and Arish Airport, serving villages, residential communities, industrial facilities, and the airport.
The project includes separate 12-kilometre railway connections to Arish Port and a cement factory. The port connection complements the Arish Port expansion, enabling goods to move between the Mediterranean gateway and the national railway network.
Engineering works include nine crossing bridges, a railway alignment bridge and two tunnels. The ministry said Transport Minister Kamel Al-Wazir also directed the construction of an underpass at Al-Mazar village to facilitate residents’ movement.
Further sections extend 85 kilometres from Arish to Al-Hasana and 173 kilometres from Al-Hasana to Taba.
Al-Wazir described the railway as a development corridor, transporting people and goods and supporting economic activity across Sinai.
The railway is a central component of the Arish–Taba logistics corridor, linking the Mediterranean with the Gulf of Aqaba through industrial and mining areas in central Sinai. According to the ministry, it will connect factories and production centres to domestic markets and export routes via the ports of Arish and Taba.
Egypt began passenger railway trials on the 100-kilometre Fardan–Bir Al-Abd section on 7 October 2024.
Egyptian National Railways operates four daily passenger journeys between Qantara East and Bir Al-Abd using upgraded Tahya Misr coaches. The service covers eight stations, providing a transport link for communities along the route.
The railway accompanies broader investment in the peninsula. Egypt allocated around EGP 35 billion for Sinai development across the 2025/2026 and 2026/2027 fiscal years.
Arish’s railway history dates to January 1917, when the British military railway being built across Sinai reached the city before extending to Rafah that March, according to Sinai heritage researcher Mahmoud Al-Shorbagy. The line subsequently carried civilian passengers and goods.
An earlier restoration project opened the Fardan–Bir Al-Abd railway in 2001 but stopped short of Arish. The current extension aims to complete that connection before continuing south toward Taba.

high_priority_articles.title: Scotland must earn its NATO place, says SNP defence MP - UK Defence Journal
high_priority_articles.summary: Scotland must earn its NATO place, says SNP defence MP  UK Defence Journal
high_priority_articles.full_text:
EXCLUSIVE – An independent Scotland would hold the Greenland Iceland gap on NATO’s behalf and would have to demonstrate what it brings to the alliance beyond its geography, the SNP Westminster leader told me when I sat down with him to chat all things defence.
Dave Doogan, the member for Angus and Perthshire Glens, said his party’s policy of NATO membership carries obligations that cannot be assumed. “You can’t just want to be in NATO. You have to demonstrate that you’re worthy to be in NATO. NATO is a collective assurance and defence pact, and so if we are asking those current members of NATO to let us into that club, then we need to know, they need to know rather, that, well, what are you going to do over and above your geography, Scotland? And we need to be able to answer that question and answer it clearly.”
The geography itself would change name and meaning on independence, and Doogan set out what that would leave Scotland responsible for in the North Atlantic approaches: “If you look at an independent Scotland, the Greenland Iceland UK gap would then be the Greenland Iceland Scotland gap, and you and I both know that the corridor of principal tension between Russia and NATO is in that environment, that Euro-Atlantic region. So Scotland would have, working with their allies, a role in that.”
Doogan argued that Scottish membership would be an addition to the alliance and not a subtraction from it. “An independent Scotland within NATO makes the United Kingdom greater than the sum of its parts. There’s an additionality with an independent Scotland. We won’t be spending that five and a half billion annually, recurring and growing, on something else. We’ll be spending it on defence of the realm and defence of the Euro-Atlantic zone in cooperation with our allies, just like Denmark does, just like Norway does, just like Finland and Sweden do, and the UK do.”
He warned against treating the Typhoon force at Lossiemouth as a Scottish asset in all but name, arguing that the station exists for a job wider than Scotland: “Let’s not think for one minute Lossiemouth is there to defend Scotland alone. Lossiemouth is there to protect the UK’s northern flank.”
Doogan has already done the arithmetic behind that offer, having drafted and costed a plan for an independent Scotland with an army, a navy and an air force funded by around five and a half billion pounds a year. He wrote it about two and a half years ago, said it now needs updating, and corrected the suggestion that the work was unfinished, saying it simply needs a refresh. He is holding it back until the next independence referendum debate.
Asked why he has not published it, he said: “All of these things are about timing, and you know we can’t all see defence as a priority. I accept that, but actually, if we unpack these things, if we don’t have security, then we don’t have anything. And security isn’t just about territorial integrity and freedom of movement. It’s about food security, energy security, and a whole range of other things.”
He added that the document is written to answer a question that has not yet been asked in earnest: “Why not release the defence plan now? Well, a good reason is that it needs a refresh, but it’s designed to answer a question when enough people are asking that question, and that will come when we’re having the next independence referendum debate. Because I believe that it’s a cogent and sensible plan.”
Doogan described the document as “a signpost and a clarion acceptance that Scotland has a responsibility to defend itself as an independent state, and it has a responsibility to be a responsive and reliable partner to our allies.”
On the shape of the force, he said the plan assumes a conventional structure built up over a number of years: “The proposal that I’ve drafted and costed shows Scotland with a traditional three main service, army, navy and air force, and of course that needs generated over time. You don’t start with that, but you can have it on the drawing board.”
The budget comes from Scotland’s existing share of British defence spending, money he says is already being spent on Scotland’s behalf: “Scotland would be in a position to spend what it currently is exposed to in terms of the UK fiscal environment on defence, which is circa five, five and a half billion per share of the UK defence budget. That would be on a rolling year-on-year recurring with inflation, a budget that would generate a substantial defence force across three services.”
Doogan argued that the headline percentage tells you very little on its own, telling me “I often think two or three per cent of GDP is pretty abstract. Sometimes it’s not what you do, it’s the way that you do it. And the same is true, it’s not what you spend, it’s what you spend it on.”
He made the case for the naval component on industrial grounds, arguing that Scotland is among a small group of countries with the yards to build its own warships: “If you look at the amount of countries around the world that could have a stab at building a complex warship, there’s about twenty maybe at a push, and Scotland’s one of them. In fact, we’ve got two sites that can build complex warships on each side of the country.”
Doogan said he would be happy to go into where an independent Scotland would source combat aircraft, train its pilots and secure interoperability, while declining to treat those as prior conditions. “These are all legitimate operational questions, which I would quite like to answer, but I don’t feel the need to answer them because actually these are challenges that every sovereign state faces, and every sovereign state has to shop around for these platforms.”
On the division of existing British military equipment, he said the ownership position is clear but the practical answer is not. “It’s important to remember that we own the assets, all of them proportionately, at the disposal of the UK defence forces, and so we’ve got a call on them. But why would we make problems for the UK by taking our share?”
He set that against the state of the British inventory, where he argues the margin for giving anything away has long gone: “You know as well as I do that there is very little redundancy in any platform in the United Kingdom. You know, just look at what they were trying to do to get a functioning Type 45 out to the Mediterranean recently. If we think that there are squadrons of Typhoons up and down these islands ready to go at a moment’s notice, that’s not how it is.”
On that basis he ruled out pressing a claim that damaged what remained of the UK, telling me “So if we were to claim our share of eight per cent or whatever of UK assets, and that caused major difficulties for the UK, well, we just wouldn’t do it because it’s not intelligent.”
Division of assets has been one of the hardest parts of the independence argument to pin down since 2014, when the Scottish Government’s white paper assumed a share of equipment would transfer and the then British government declined to negotiate before a vote. The eight per cent figure Doogan uses reflects Scotland’s rough share of the British population, which was the basis the 2014 prospectus worked from.
On relations with what would remain of the United Kingdom, Doogan expects cooperation to follow from mutual interest. “Let’s not pretend for one minute that the United Kingdom, once all the heat has gone out of an independence debate and Scotland has chosen to be independent, the rest of the UK will cooperate with Scotland just in the same way it cooperates with every other entity and jurisdiction that used to be governed from London. It’s entirely predictable, because it’s to England’s and the rest of the UK’s self interest to cooperate with Scotland, and it’s in Scotland’s interest to cooperate with the rest of the UK.”
He added that the hostility between the two governments is a product of the constitutional argument itself: “This enmity that exists just now is a function of trying to keep the UK together. Once Scotland’s out of the UK, that enmity has no purpose anymore, and we’ll work together like grown-up and respectful states.”
Doogan said that losing jurisdiction over the northern half of the island would present the rest of the UK with a problem, and that he would not want it handled adversarially. “If the SNP or I have got anything to do with that, that won’t be a challenge because we’ll approach it in a cooperative way. How we do that is up for discussion. A brand new independent Scotland would not want to be undefended, but the rest of the UK would not wish a brand new independent Scotland to be undefended either.”
On the deterrent, he said Scotland would have no further say once the system left Scottish waters. “We have got no locus with the deterrent once it’s removed from Scottish waters. It’s not a Scottish asset or system, it’s a UK asset or system. And so what they choose to do with it, where they choose to berth it, whether they choose to sustain and renew it going forward into the future, that’s entirely up to the rest of the UK. Scotland will have no role in that. We’ll respect their sovereignty and their freedom of decision, and they’ll respect ours.”
Where the deterrent goes after independence would be settled in London, and Doogan accepts Scotland would have no say in it once the system leaves Scottish waters. The rest of the case is his to make, and it comes down to a navy and air force built around the North Atlantic, five and a half billion a year spent on conventional defence, and a neighbour the alliance can rely on. On his own test, that is what Scotland would have to show over and above its geography. He says he has the plan to prove it, and he is waiting for the moment to publish it.
Doogan spent his career in defence engineering before entering Parliament in 2019 and has pushed conventional defence up the SNP’s agenda, work he describes as still in progress.

high_priority_articles.title: Securing equipment emerges as new variable for Korea's chip expansion plans - The Korea Times
high_priority_articles.summary: Securing equipment emerges as new variable for Korea's chip expansion plans  The Korea Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
ASML not accepting orders for 2029, 2030
Securing equipment for manufacturing advanced memory chips is emerging as a new variable in Korea's plans to expand semiconductor production capacity through large-scale industrial clusters, after ASML, the dominant supplier of advanced chipmaking equipment, warned that its current production plans may not be sufficient to meet demand in 2027 and 2028.
During its earnings call Wednesday, ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet said the company's plans to increase its production capacity for advanced chipmaking equipment by 30 percent in 2027 and another 30 percent in 2028 would likely not be enough to meet customer demand.
“Last quarter, we talked about 30 percent more capacity next year, and also the aspiration to have another 30 percent increase in 2028,” Fouquet said. “But to be honest, it's becoming very clear that 30 percent in 2027, 30 percent in 2028 will not allow us to meet our customer demand.”
According to the company, the planned capacity increases cover both low-numerical-aperture extreme ultraviolet (low-NA EUV) lithography equipment and deep ultraviolet (DUV) immersion systems.
EUV equipment is used to produce extremely fine circuit patterns for advanced semiconductor chips, while DUV immersion systems are used for a broader range of patterning processes. Both are critical to manufacturing high-performance memory chips produced by companies such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix.
“So a lot of our discussions with our customers now are shifting in fact beyond 2027,” Fouquet said. “A lot of order intake for 2028. But also some strong interest to already place orders for 2029 and sometimes even 2030."
The supply bottleneck anticipated by ASML could become a major variable in Korea's ongoing plans to build large-scale semiconductor industrial complexes in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province, and Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City.
In Yongin, two separate semiconductor clusters are planned, each housing fabrication facilities of SK hynix and Samsung Electronics. SK hynix has already begun construction of its fabrication facilities, while Samsung is scheduled to break ground later this month. Separately, the two companies plan to build large-scale semiconductor manufacturing sites in Jeonnam-Gwangju, upon the government’s push.
The two companies declined to confirm the status of their equipment orders, but industry officials said a supply bottleneck could materialize if strong demand persists beyond 2030.
“It is difficult to describe the current situation as a bottleneck. Given that ASML is expanding its production capacity, it is hard to expect that orders placed now would face delays significant enough to call it a bottleneck,” an industry official said. “However, if the current strong demand persists over the long term, supply bottlenecks could emerge.”
In the semiconductor industry, the lead time for equipment orders — the period between placing an order and receiving the equipment — typically ranges from 18 months to two years. This suggests that the current supply situation largely reflects orders placed around 2025.
The concern is that supply bottlenecks could materialize if demand remains strong or continues to grow through 2028, 2029 and 2030, coinciding with Korea's planned fab expansions.
In Yongin, SK hynix is targeting October next year for the start of production at its first fab, with equipment deliveries expected to accelerate as construction of additional fabs pick up speed. Samsung Electronics is also planning to begin operations at its first Yongin fab in 2029.
The outlook is more uncertain for the cluster in Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City.
Although neither company has officially announced a construction or operation schedule for their planned fabs in the region, local authorities are targeting the start of construction next year and mass production in 2030. This means that if demand remains strong in the coming years, equipment deliveries to the planned facilities could face bottlenecks.
Against the backdrop, ASML Chief Financial Officer Roger Dassen told analysts that ASML is holding off on accepting orders for 2029 and 2030 while it assesses both customers' readiness and its own ability to meet future demand.
"We don't want now to accept orders from customer A, B and C and then to tell customer D, who hasn't given orders yet for 2029 and 2030, 'Sorry, we're sold out,'" Dassen told analysts on the post-earnings call.
“While policy support for the Jeonnam-Gwangju clusters has largely focused on speeding up land development and power supply, securing equipment could emerge as a new variable in how quickly the fabs come online,” another industry official said.
